text: Previtali trained under Giovanni Bellini and spent most of his career in Bergamo, where he's also recorded as Andrea Cordelliaghi. His altarpieces there include a John the Baptist preaching with other saints for the church of Santo Spirito, and a Deposition for Sant'Andrea. In 1937 Kenneth Clark, then director of the National Gallery in London, bought two small panels of his from a dealer in Vienna. Clark paid £14,000 and his curators objected. The British press noticed Previtali that year mostly because he wasn't Giorgione. He died in 1528.

According to the RKD, Elias Vonck worked in Poland for about eight years, and his son Jan was born there. Vonck himself was an Amsterdam man, born in 1605 and dead in 1652. He painted portraits, still lifes, hunting scenes and farm scenes with animals. The site holds his Dead Wild Fowl from 1640. He belongs to the Dutch Golden Age.

David de Coninck rarely signed his pictures, so his animal paintings have often been mistaken for work by Boel, Fyt and even Snijders. He was born in Antwerp around 1644 and learned from Pieter Boel. In Rome he joined the Bentvueghels, a club of Dutch and Flemish artists, and took the nickname Rammelaer, which means rattle. He also worked for several years in Paris and for a time in Vienna. The last record of him is from Brussels in 1701. Nobody knows when or where he died.

Karel van Mander wrote that Dirck Barendsz was "nursed at the great Titian's bosom." Barendsz trained with his father, a painter known as deaf Barent, and then spent seven years in Italy from 1555. In Rome he met Philip van Marnix, who became a great friend. His chapel piece for the Amsterdam militia was destroyed in the Beeldenstorm. The Christmas piece in Gouda is the only complete altarpiece of his that survives. He died in Amsterdam in 1592.

Yun Shouping was born to a poor family in Wujin, in Jiangsu province, and they couldn't afford to send him to the civil service examinations. So he turned to art. He began as a landscape painter, but he was reportedly so impressed by Wang Hui that he switched to flowers, animals and insects. He copied the boneless method of Xu Xi, which tried to do without hard outlines. He also used reds and purples that Chinese painters had long thought gaudy. He died in 1690, and people count him among the Six Masters of the early Qing.

Oda Krohg grew up with eight sisters and two brothers, and her brother Per Lasson became a composer. She started studying painting in 1885 with Erik Werenskiold and Christian Krohg. She married Krohg in 1888. The family later lived in Berlin and in Paris. In an etching by Edvard Munch of a cafe interior, she sits among the bohemians. Her son Per also became a notable painter.

In 1902 Eugeniusz Zak left Warsaw for Paris to study under Jean-Léon Gérôme at the École des Beaux-Arts. He later moved to the Académie Colarossi. He also spent time in Munich at a private school run by the Slovenian Anton Ažbe. His Paris debut came at the Autumn Salon, and the French state bought one of his paintings for the Musée du Luxembourg. Zak was born into a Jewish family in Mogilno, now in Belarus, and he died in January 1926.

Harmen Steenwijck never dated his paintings, so the dates of his work have to be estimated. He was born in Delft around 1612, the son of an eyeglass maker. Around 1628 he went to Leiden to live and study with his uncle David Bailly, who's credited with inventing the vanitas genre. His brother Pieter was a still-life painter too. Harmen set his objects out on a table in a diagonal or a triangle. His best known picture, An Allegory of the Vanities of Human Life, is in the National Gallery in London.

Jacopo Guarana is said to have studied under Sebastiano Ricci and then Giovanni Battista Tiepolo. He was born in Verona in 1720 but worked mostly in Venice, where he was a founding member of the Accademia di Belle Arti. His frescoes can be found at Ca' Rezzonico and in the concert hall of the Ospedaletto. He also decorated several Venetian palaces. His son Vincenzo, born in 1742, became a painter too. Guarana died in 1808.

Ferraù Fenzoni went by two nicknames, Ferraù da Faenza and Il Faenzone, both after his birthplace. He moved to Rome in the early 1580s and worked on fresco cycles under Sixtus V, including the Scala Santa and the Sistine library. From 1594 he worked in Todi, where most of his cathedral murals are lost except for a Last Judgement. He then went back to Faenza and stayed there for the rest of his career. A Deposition for his own chapel in a church that has since been destroyed was one of his last big paintings. He died in 1645.

Self-taught in Nottingham, Thomas Sandby ran a drawing academy with his brother Paul before the two went to London in 1741. In 1743 he became private secretary and draughtsman to the Duke of Cumberland and followed him on campaigns in Flanders and Scotland. The duke later made him Deputy Ranger of Windsor Great Park, where he did a good deal of landscaping. Sandby was a founding member of the Royal Academy and its first professor of architecture. His best known building, Freemasons' Hall in London, has been demolished. He died in 1798.

Wincenty Dmochowski opened a private painting school in Vilnius in 1840, and Józef Marszewski was one of his best-known students. He had studied painting at Vilnius University under Jan Rustem. After taking part in the November Uprising he had to go into exile in Prussia, and an amnesty let him return. He's known mostly for landscapes, but he also painted historical scenes, portraits and rural interiors. One series of canvases was based on the poetry of Adam Mickiewicz. His son Władysław became a well-known painter too.

Carl Julius von Leypold painted Wanderer in the Storm, the picture he's best known for. He studied landscape painting with Johan Christian Dahl at the Dresden Academy of Fine Arts. From 1826 Caspar David Friedrich shaped his choice of subjects and his style. His landscapes are painterly but sharp-brushed, with the objectivity of the Biedermeier period. The Dresden academy made him an honorary member in 1857. He died in 1874.

Cornelius Høyer learned miniature painting in Paris from Jean-Baptiste Massé. Before that he had studied at the Royal Danish Academy of Fine Arts under Carl Gustaf Pilo and Louis Tocqué. A visit to Italy in 1767 brought him to Rosalba Carriera, and he picked up new skills there, among them painting on ivory. In 1769 he became Miniature Painter to the Danish Court. Later visits to the courts in Stockholm, Saint Petersburg and Berlin built his name abroad. Born at the Kronborg Rifle Factory, he died in 1804.

The Augsburg engraver Andreas Matthäus Wolfgang had two sons, and the elder, Gustav Andreas, was taught in Berlin by his uncle Johann Georg Wolfgang. His brother Christian followed him there, and Gustav taught him in turn. Gustav later went back to Augsburg, where he was born in 1692 and where he lived until his death in 1775. He worked as a painter and engraver, and the British Museum holds his prints. One of his portraits shows Johann Albert Fabricius and is dated 1749.

Ichiryūsai Yoshitoyo started out studying with Utagawa Kunisada, then left him and joined Kuniyoshi's studio. Kunisada had just taken the name Toyokuni, and Kuniyoshi gave his new pupil the name Yoshitoyo on purpose, with the same two characters turned around. Yoshitoyo drew warrior prints, measles prints and kite pictures, and later Yokohama prints of foreigners. Some prints from 1863 show an elephant newly brought to Japan. He died in 1866 at 37.

Charles Prendergast made picture frames before he made pictures. As a custom woodworker in Boston he carved frames by hand for the leading artists of his day, John Singer Sargent among them. He was born in St. John's, Newfoundland, in 1863, and the family moved to Boston when he was a child. After a trip to Italy with his brother Maurice in 1911 he began painting too, when he was almost fifty. His first painting, Rising Sun, was on a carved wood and gesso panel.

Francisco Pacheco is best remembered as the teacher of Alonso Cano and Diego Velázquez, and Velázquez became his son-in-law. He was born in Sanlúcar de Barrameda and moved to Seville shortly before 1580, taking the name of his uncle, the dean of Seville Cathedral. He learned a lot by copying Italian masters. His book Art of Painting, published after his death, is an important source on how painters worked in 17th-century Spain. Some call him the Vasari of Seville, outspoken about theory but conventional in his own pictures. He died in 1644.

Among the drawings of Jean-Jacques Lequeu is a cow barn in the shape of an Assyrian bull. After the Revolution his architectural career never took off, and he worked as a surveyor and cartographer in the civil service until 1815. His book Architecture Civile was never published. Most of his drawings are now in the Bibliothèque nationale de France. The Viennese historian Emil Kaufmann rediscovered him in the middle of the 20th century, and the first monograph on him came out in 1986. Lequeu died in Paris in 1826.

Two rulers of the Netherlands hired Louis-Marie Autissier as court painter, first Louis Bonaparte and later Willem I. Born in Vannes in Brittany, he joined the revolutionary army and was soon noticed for his drawing. He settled in Brussels in 1796 and became famous for miniature portraits of sovereigns, nobles and celebrities. In 1817 he painted the Duke of Wellington. He's considered the founder of the Belgian school of miniature painting in the 19th century. He died in 1830.

Ernst Grünewald learned copper engraving in Darmstadt from Johann Conrad Susemihl, then in Karlsruhe from Karl Ludwig Frommel. In Karlsruhe he also found backers for his poetry, and a volume of his verse came out in 1827. After he went home he became court engraver. Together with the Englishman William John Cooke he ran a workshop under the name Grünewald & Cooke, which turned more and more to steel engraving for books. He died in Darmstadt in 1848.

Oskari Paatela began in agriculture and forestry at the University of Helsinki, took drawing lessons from Eero Järnefelt, and then gave up his degree for art. In 1910 he went to Paris with the painter Eero Snellman and studied at the Académie Colarossi. His style ranged from realism in the manner of Anders Zorn to an elegant decorative look. He painted altarpieces for the churches in Virolahti and Alavus, and a fresco for the YMCA hall in Helsinki. After his wife died in 1927 he drank heavily and his work faded away. His brothers Jussi and Toivo were well-known architects.

The son of a shoemaker, Carl Frederik Aagaard had his first painting lessons in Odense. In 1852 he moved to Copenhagen to join his brother, a woodcutter. There Georg Hilker taught him decorative painting, and he also learned to draw on wood and to etch. Later he studied landscape with P. C. Skovgaard. Many of his pictures show places that tourists visited. The architect Vilhelm Dahlerup designed his house, using stones from the old Royal Danish Theatre. Aagaard became a professor in 1892.

Nobody knows where Gakuō Zōkyū came from or who his family was. He was a Zen monk who painted in the late Muromachi period, and about 20 of his later works are known. He seems to have been close to the Tōfuku-ji temple in Kyoto, where the high priest Ryōan Keigo praised one of his paintings. A text from 1486 lists him as a pupil of Shūbun, so he probably took over the ink painting method of that line. His landscapes are loose in style and often heavy with black ink.

Canova's father, a stonecutter, died when he was a small child, and his grandfather Pasino, a stonemason, took over his training. Before he was ten he was already making clay models and carving marble. His first marble statue, Daedalus and Icarus, earned him 100 gold zecchini, and one idea is that Daedalus has his grandfather's face. In 1780 he arrived in Rome on a three-year pension from the Venetian Senate. There he sketched Michelangelo's works, and the Venetian ambassador hired him to carve Theseus and the Minotaur. He died in 1822.

A second cousin of the poet Émile Verhaeren, Alfred Verhaeren was first placed with an architect to learn drawing plans. He quit to study at the Brussels academy under Jean-François Portaels and Louis Dubois, and he copied old master still lifes to perfect his technique. He joined La Chrysalide, founded in 1875, alongside James Ensor and Constantin Meunier. Later he showed with Les XX. In 1885 he joined Voorwaarts, a young artists' group with a Dutch name and the motto Hooger is ons doel. He painted portraits, interiors, architecture and still lifes, and he died in Ixelles in 1924.

Herman van Lin signed his first known painting in 1649, and nothing is recorded about his life before that. He was probably born in Utrecht. He may have gone to Rome, where Dutch painters knew him as De Stille, the peaceful one, but doubts remain about that trip. From 1659 or earlier he was a member of the Utrecht painters' guild, and he was elected its dean four times. He painted landscapes and battle scenes, and the Prado has his Cavalry Battle. He probably died a little before February 1681 at the fortress of Schenkenschans.

Doctors told James Dickson Innes to travel after he was diagnosed with tuberculosis, so much of his work was done abroad, mainly at Collioure in France but also in Spain and Morocco. Born in Llanelli in south Wales, he studied at the Slade under Henry Tonks and P. Wilson Steer. In 1911 he joined the Camden Town Group. He painted around Arenig Fawr in North Wales with Augustus John, who remembered him in a Quaker hat, a coloured silk scarf and a long black overcoat. Innes died of the disease in 1914 at 27.

Jasper van der Lanen's work was rediscovered only in the middle of the 20th century. Very little is known about his life. He was a pupil of the obscure painter Nicolaas Geerts and later a master of the Antwerp guild. When his friend Abraham Govaerts, another young landscape painter, died in 1626, Van der Lanen was one of the artists asked to finish Govaerts's unfinished pictures. Many of his wooded landscapes with figures had been given to others, such as Jan Brueghel the Younger, until signed works turned up. Nobody knows exactly when he died.

Prince Rupert of the Rhine commanded the Royalist cavalry in the English Civil War, and he also made mezzotints. He was the third son of Frederick V of the Palatinate and Elizabeth, daughter of James VI and I. After a quarrel with the exiled Royalist court he went to Germany. The critic Antony Griffiths calls his print The Great Executioner one of the greatest mezzotints. Later Rupert was a founding member of the Royal Society and fitted out a laboratory at Windsor Castle. He died in 1682.

George Catlin practiced law for two years before giving it up to travel and study art. His mother had been captured by Indians in the Battle of Wyoming, and her stories fascinated him as a boy. In 1830 he went up the Mississippi with Governor William Clark, and from St. Louis he made five trips, eventually visiting fifty tribes. He also went more than 3,000 km up the Missouri to Fort Union and stayed several weeks. He died in 1872.

Leonetto Cappiello had no formal art training and started out as a satirical caricaturist. His first album of caricatures, Lanterna Magica, came out in 1896, and two years later he moved to Paris for good. He made his name with posters, each built around one bright, often surreal figure against a flat dark background. Earlier poster artists such as Jules Chéret and Alphonse Mucha had used detailed, painterly backdrops. He's often called the father of modern advertising. Cappiello died in 1942.

Eugène Flandin drew the monuments and street life of Iran while travelling with the architect Pascal Coste. The two joined a French embassy to Iran. Then they went on to Isfahan, Shiraz and Tabriz with very little money. Coste praised Flandin's courage and also noted his violent temper. Afterwards Flandin was sent to draw the Assyrian remains Paul-Émile Botta had found at Khorsabad, and he took part in the excavations there. He was born in Naples in 1809 and died in Tours in 1889.

Antiquity Smith, as John Thomas Smith came to be called, tried to train as a sculptor with Joseph Nollekens but left for John Keyse Sherwin and the Royal Academy. In 1807 he published Antiquities of Westminster. It grew out of paintings found at the Houses of Parliament, which he sketched early in the morning to avoid the workmen. They kept demolishing what he had just drawn. He also became the young John Constable's informal mentor. Smith himself was born in the back of a Hackney carriage.

Audubon set out to make a picture record of every bird species in North America. The result was The Birds of America, engraved in Scotland and England on huge double elephant folio sheets, with five volumes of text to go with it. Born Jean-Jacques Rabin on a sugarcane plantation in Les Cayes, in what is now Haiti, he was accused of fraud and plagiarism during his life. He has also been criticized for buying and selling slaves. More than two dozen regional Audubon societies have since changed their names.

Jan van de Velde is better known for his etching and engraving than for his painting. His father was the calligrapher Jan van de Velde the Elder from Antwerp, and he trained with the engraver Jacob Matham. In 1616 he drew Haarlem scenes as a series of 26 landscape prints. Thirty years later he expanded it to 60, and most of them are in the North Holland Archives. Houbraken says Esaias van de Velde was his brother, while another writer calls Esaias a cousin. He died in Enkhuizen in 1641.

Matthäus Merian the Elder learned copperplate engraving in Zürich and then worked in Strasbourg, Nancy and Paris. In 1617 he married Maria Magdalena de Bry, the daughter of a publisher, and in 1623 he took over her father's publishing house in Frankfurt. With the geographer Martin Zeiler he produced the Topographia, a set of 21 volumes. Early on he had drawn detailed town plans of Basel and Paris. His daughter Anna Maria Sibylla Merian became a pioneering naturalist and illustrator. He died in 1650.

Monks were Eduard von Grützner's favourite subject, and he painted Falstaff again and again. A local pastor noticed his talent as a boy and got him into the Carolinum in Neisse, then took him to Munich for art school in 1864. He joined Piloty's class at the Munich Academy and left after three years. In 1870 he moved into his own studio and soon did very well. The Bavarian prince regent gave him the title of professor, and he was knighted in 1916.

Józef Mehoffer worked for more than 40 years on the stained glass windows of the St Nicholas Collegiate Church in Fribourg, Switzerland. He studied painting at the academy in Kraków under Władysław Łuszczkiewicz, then in Vienna and Paris. He also designed stained glass for chapels and churches across Poland, as well as textiles, etchings, theatre sets and furniture. He often worked with Stanisław Wyspiański and Jan Matejko. Mehoffer died in Wadowice in 1946.

William Glackens worked as an illustrator for newspapers and magazines in Philadelphia and New York while he was also painting. He was one of the founders of the Ashcan School, which rejected the formal boundaries of beauty laid down by the conservative National Academy of Design. His dark street scenes of New York and Paris first made his name, and his later work got brighter under the influence of Renoir. He helped Albert C. Barnes buy the European paintings at the core of the Barnes Foundation. His older brother Louis was a cartoonist.

Herman Saftleven the Younger painted river views and travellers in woods. Born in Rotterdam, he lived most of his life in Utrecht, where he became dean of the Guild of St Luke. After a storm in 1674 destroyed most of the town, he sold the city a series of drawings of Utrecht churches he had made before they were wrecked. In the 1680s the botanist Agnes Block hired him to draw flowers and plants at her country estate. His brother Cornelis was better known as a painter, and his daughter Sara painted flowers in watercolour. He died in Utrecht in 1685.

Friedrich Weinbrenner started out as an apprentice to his father, a carpenter in Karlsruhe. He spent five years in Italy studying the ancient buildings of Rome, Pompeii, Herculaneum and Paestum, and he was among the first German architects to see the early Doric temples at Paestum. Back home he settled in Karlsruhe as its official architect and, beginning with his 1797 General Plan, shaped it as a classical city. A generation of architects trained under him. He died in 1826.

Jan de Visscher made prints after famous Haarlem painters such as Berchem, Adriaen van Ostade and Jan van Goyen. According to Houbraken, he took up painting at 56, as a pupil of the landscape painter Michiel Carrée. No paintings by him are known. The RKD says his brothers were Cornelis and Lambert de Visscher. He was registered in Amsterdam in 1692, but nobody recorded his death. Houbraken wrote about him in the past tense, so he's assumed to have died before 1712.

Both of William Orpen's parents painted as amateurs, and he grew up the youngest of four sons of a Dublin solicitor. He worked mostly in London and was a popular portrait painter for well-off Edwardian society. In the First World War he was the most prolific of the official war artists on the Western Front. His army connections let him stay in France longer than any of the others. It cost him his health and his social standing in Britain. After his early death, critics dismissed his work, and his paintings were rarely shown until the 1980s.

Willem van de Velde the Younger painted the sea battles his father drew. The elder Van de Velde was an experienced draughtsman who prepared black and white studies of battles and seascapes, and the son worked them up in oils. War with the French pushed them out of the Netherlands, and in England Charles II engaged both of them at a salary of £100. Willem had already become famous before he came to London. The Duke of York was another patron.

In Russia Jan Ciągliński was known as fierce Jan, because he worked so fast and with such passion. This Polish painter was active in St. Petersburg, helped found the Mir iskusstva group, and later taught at the Imperial Academy. His students included Ivan Bilibin, Pavel Filonov and Yury Annenkov. He also painted Orientalist scenes from sketches made on long trips through North Africa and the Middle East. Many of his portraits show musicians, among them Tchaikovsky and Rachmaninoff. He died in 1913.

Aubrey Beardsley caught tuberculosis at seven. It killed him in 1898, at 25. His black ink drawings were influenced by Japanese woodcuts and dealt in the grotesque, the decadent and the erotic. He belonged to the aesthetic movement, in the same circle as Oscar Wilde and James McNeill Whistler. His father had no trade and lived off an inheritance, and the family moved from Brighton to London in 1883. Beardsley contributed a good deal to Art Nouveau and poster styles.

Wang Meng spent the last five years of his life in jail, falsely accused of plotting against the Ming emperor Taizu. His maternal grandfather was Zhao Mengfu. Wang is counted among the Four Masters of the Yuan dynasty, along with Huang Gongwang, Wu Zhen and Ni Zan, who refused to serve the Mongol rulers. All four painted only landscapes, mostly on paper instead of silk. Wang was the youngest and the least famous in his own time. His ropy brushstrokes, piled one on another into dense texture, still influenced later painters. He died in 1385.

Carl Blechen's parents couldn't afford more schooling, so they apprenticed him to a banker, and he stayed in banking until he went to the Berlin Academy in 1822. He found work as a stage decorator at the Royal Theater and lost it after a dispute with the singer Henriette Sontag. A trip to Italy gave him hundreds of sketches, which he worked up later in his Berlin studio. The landscapes there changed his whole manner of painting. Karl Friedrich Schinkel recommended him as professor of landscape painting. He died in 1840.

People sometimes called David Wilkie the people's painter. His father, a parish minister in Fife, reluctantly agreed in 1799 to let him become a painter. Wilkie worked mostly in London on genre scenes, historical subjects and royal portraits, and he became Principal Painter in Ordinary to William IV and then to Queen Victoria. His best-known painting today is probably The Chelsea Pensioners reading the Waterloo Dispatch, in Apsley House. He died on the way home from his first trip to the Middle East and was buried at sea off Gibraltar.

Roelant Savery was about four when his Anabaptist family fled north from the Spanish-held southern Netherlands and settled in Haarlem. He learned painting from his older brother Jacob and from Hans Bol. Around 1604 he went to Prague as court painter to the emperors Rudolf II and Matthias, and later he traveled to Tyrol to study plants. In Utrecht he bought a big house with a garden of flowers and plants, where fellow painters often visited. He was buried in 1639.

Jan van Huysum was secretive about his method and worked apart from the rest of his family of painters. Trained in decoration from a young age, he lived mostly in Amsterdam. One old description says you can see drops of water and crawling ants in his flower pieces without a magnifying glass. He and his wife had 12 children, and only three outlived their parents. His daughter Francina also painted flowers, and Margareta Haverman studied with him until she moved to Paris. He died in 1749.

August von Pettenkofen gave up a military career to study at the Vienna academy under Leopold Kupelwieser and Franz Eybl. In the revolutions of 1848 he became a military painter. Szolnok in Hungary left a deep impression on him, and his style became more picturesque. Paris followed, and with it the influence of the Barbizon school. He painted the uneventful, melancholy lives of Hungarian peasants and Roma without theatrical pathos or forced humour. Venice he visited every year. He was knighted in 1876 and died in Vienna in 1889.

Apollinary Vasnetsov had no formal artistic education and studied under his older brother Viktor. From 1883 the two lived and worked in Abramtsevo, where Vasily Polenov influenced him. He specialised in scenes from the medieval history of Moscow, and he built his own genre of historical landscape reconstruction on historical and archaeological data. In 1890 he travelled across the north of the Russian Empire and recorded views of Siberia and the Urals. He joined the Peredvizhniki in 1899. Later he helped found the Union of Russian Artists.

Abbott Handerson Thayer is best known for his angel paintings, some of which use his own children as models. He grew up in rural New Hampshire near Mount Monadnock, where he called himself bird crazy, hunted and trapped, and studied Audubon's Birds of America. Late in life he and his son Gerald wrote a book on protective coloration in nature, which may have had an effect on military camouflage in World War I. Theodore Roosevelt and others mocked it for assuming that all animal coloration is cryptic. He also taught apprentices in his studio and died in 1921.

Only 14 of Gabriël Metsu's 133 works are dated. His mother was a poor midwife, and his stepfather, a skipper, probably paid for his schooling. He grew up in Leiden on the Lange Mare and was among the first members of the painters' guild there in 1648. Around 1655 he moved to Amsterdam, to an alley on the Prinsengracht next to a brewery. He painted history scenes, still lifes, portraits and genre scenes, and never stuck with one style for long. He died in 1667.

Johannes Jelgerhuis worked as both a painter and an actor. He studied with his father Rienk Jelgerhuis and with Pieter Pietersz Barbiers. From 1808 he acted at the Stadsschouwburg in Amsterdam and wrote an illustrated instruction booklet for actors. In 1820 he began teaching acting and asked his former colleague Johanna Wattier to help. As a painter he made interiors and architectural studies, and he had a good eye for perspective. His picture of his publisher's bookshop is in the Rijksmuseum. He died in Amsterdam in 1836.

Mattia Preti was nicknamed Il Cavalier Calabrese, the Calabrian Knight, after the Knights of Malta made him a knight in 1660. He came from Taverna, a small town in Calabria, the third child in a middle-class family. As a boy he was put in the care of the parish priest, Don Marcello Anania, who taught him grammar and the humanities. In 1630 he moved to Rome to live with his older brother Gregorio, also a painter. Preti worked in Italy and Malta, and he died in 1699.

Domenico Beccafumi's father was a peasant on the estate of Lorenzo Beccafumi, who noticed the boy's talent for drawing and adopted him. Domenico went to Rome but soon came back to Siena. Two Sienese painters of his generation, Il Sodoma and Peruzzi, picked up the Florentine-Umbrian classical style in Rome, but his own style stayed provincial. He painted religious pieces for churches and mythological scenes for private patrons. From 1517 to 1544 he directed work on the pavement of Siena Cathedral. He died in 1551.
